The girl in question is distantly related to me, who I met for the first time recently, though we didn't talk much. She's a very nice sort of girl, Christian upbringing, protected by her parents but not in a bad way. I am thinking of sending the letter below as an email to an intermediary relative who knows her quite well, but am wondering if this is the best course of action.

Dear XXXXXXX,

I will keep the point of this message to the following paragraph, with the rest not being necessary to read, but added nonetheless to demonstrate I know what I am talking about. This message is not sent in confidence and may be shared at your discretion.

I have been mulling this over each day since I learned YYYYYYY may choose to study Psychology in the coming years. My concerns are not with the field as a whole (as you may guess from my mention of Jordan Peterson in our conversation a few days ago I have a respect for the subject), rather in where and from whom she will receive her teaching, especially at university level. Psychology, like most other social sciences, has become infested with post-modern influences, a doctrine that is both seductive and destructive. At best a post-modernist ends up nihilistic, as post-modernism actively asks its student to question and ultimately tear down their value structures. In my time at Cambridge I have seen a vast number of highly intelligent young people who have been damaged by the doctrine, many becoming hostile to traditional values, some questioning their sexuality, others being entrapped by the delusion of transsexuality. Courses and classes can typically be identified as post-modern by their course-descriptions – if unusual words are used, usually reformulations or combinations of existing words, and only a few years old, then it is highly likely the professor is a post-modernist. My suggestion here is for you to carefully consider my concerns before talking to ZZZZZZZ, but I trust you to come up with an appropriate response, even if that response is no response at all.

Post-modernism was incepted by the French intellectuals Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, Martin Heidegger, and others, who were themselves students of Marxist teachings in the mid-twentieth century. When faced with the genocidal consequences of communism, these intellectuals did what could be described as a rebranding of the same principles. Post-modernism is an answer to the problem that any piece of writing can be interpreted in many ways (some say infinitely many ways), which itself begs the question of which interpretation is correct. The answer according to post-modernism is that all interpretations are valid, and everyone chooses their interpretation to pursue their own agenda, specifically suggesting that traditional interpretations are a tool by the powerful to oppress the powerless (this is the key to the Marxist origins to the doctrine. Compare this to the Bourgeois versus Proletariat representation in Das Kapital).

The reason the axiom of equal validity of interpretation is dangerous is that it leaves no room to exclude interpretations that are pathological, it even encourages its student to consider even these interpretations with serious thought. This process of undermining one’s foundations and replacing them with harmful ideas often causes depression, which has been self-evident to me by the sheer emphasis on mental health support that students demanded. The logical conclusions of these lines of reasoning are either nihilism by the rejection of moral value systems, or destructive behaviour as is self-evident by observing social justice activists.

Unusual words in post-modern writing serve multiple purposes. First, it allows the writer or lecturer to position themselves as intellectually superior, achieving this by making the reader or listener feel like author knows something they do not, when they use unfamiliar terminology with confidence. Second, it allows the post-modernist to frame the discussion. This is best explained with a few examples.

“Decolonisation” – when I ran for student union, I heard I girl I knew (who read Psychology by the way) use this word in her speech, along the lines of “I will help other activists in our goal of decolonising this university”. That was the first time I had encountered the word outside of the internet, but it was clear that the rest of the room was familiar with this word (mostly only humanities and social science students are interested in student politics). The word implies that the institution that she was talking about was bad (and by association, “colonisation” is bad) and needs to be torn down to rectify the problem. In this the word helps frame the debate by inherently stating the object is problematic and the solution – its destruction.

“Microaggression” – derived from the same root as the micromort which is a statistical measure of probability of death e.g. skydiving has a cost of 7 micromorts, or equivalently has a 7 in a million chance of resulting in death. The word is used in situations when physical aggression has not taken place, yet some action has occurred that when combined with other similar situations would be equivalent to physical aggression. A typical example given is asking a foreigner where they came from, as this supposedly makes them feel like an “other”. Using this word frames the debate by implying that the notion that words are as harmful as physical action is valid. Sticks and stones may break my bones and mean words can hurt me as well.

“Gender” – a word whose modern definition originated in a social science department thanks to John Money in the 1950s. Prior to this, the word has been in everyday use as a polite substitute for “sex”, with the more modern understanding of the word becoming widespread due to feminism in the 1970s. The way this word frames the debate is by allowing the possibility of a definitional difference between it and the word “sex” (which can only be male or female by the presence or absence of the Y chromosome respectively). Recently it has been suggested that whilst sex is biologically determined, gender is a social construct (I remember this argument being used on BBC News, on TV shows, and in conversations with other Cambridge students), which is the foundation of the transsexual argument, that someone could be “trapped” in the body of the wrong gender.

Third, the use of these unusual words embodies the notion that controlling the words people use in turn controls the ideas of those people. This is a concept that is well developed in Orwell’s 1984 with the use of newspeak.

To sum up, post-modernism is an enticing, yet destructive doctrine, whose effects I have witnessed at my time at university. I believe it is especially seductive for people about my age because this is when we are trying to figure out life and the world, and it supplies an elegant answer as a first impression. It is especially powerful in a university setting where your company is largely comprised of other students listening to the same lecturers, reinforcing the ideas outside the lecture hall through assignments that are graded according to the philosophy. That is why it is important to make sure the course she takes is a conventional psychology course.
